name: Brain.fm
tagline: Streaming music engineered with rhythmic modulation that is supposed to push your brain into focus, relaxation, or sleep.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The mechanism Brain.fm sells is not exotic: layered ambient audio with amplitude modulation in a target frequency band, plus a session timer. Web Audio API does amplitude modulation, filtered noise, and evolving pads in a couple hundred lines, and a coding agent can get you a running generative focus player in one sitting. What it cannot generate is music anyone actually wants to listen to for eight hours: Brain.fm's catalog is composed by humans and then processed, and your synth pads will sound like a synth pad after twenty minutes. You also lose the mobile apps, offline playback, and the pile of studies they cite. Build it if you mostly want the modulated hum and a timer, keep paying if you care about the tracks.
coreLoopDIY: A local web player that generates layered ambient audio with adjustable amplitude modulation in focus, relax, and sleep bands, with session timers and volume mixing.
requirements: A modern browser with Web Audio API
Optional: a folder of your own ambient or instrumental tracks to run through the modulator
Headphones, since the effect leans on stereo and low frequency modulation
whatYouLose: A human-composed catalog with real variety, so your version gets boring fast
Native iOS and Android apps with background playback and offline downloads
Their tuned modulation depth and phase design, which is more careful than a naive LFO
Curated session types, genre choices, and any sense of discovery
The research and placebo scaffolding that makes people believe it is working, which is not nothing
moatNotes: The technical trick is copyable in an afternoon. The composed and processed music library, plus the studies people cite when defending the subscription, are not.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the product is a listening experience, not an audio effect. Brain.fm works when you press play and forget it exists for three hours, and that requires hundreds of tracks that are pleasant, non-distracting, and consistently mixed, which is a music production operation rather than a coding problem. Add native apps for phones, offline caching for planes, and a brand story with clinical citations attached, and roughly ten dollars a month is an easy yes for someone who already believes it helps them concentrate. The DIY build is a good way to find out whether you actually respond to modulated audio or just like having a focus ritual.
notes: The generator is a one-sitting build; the reason you keep listening is the catalog.
prompt:
Build a local, single-page focus audio player called "Modulate" using plain HTML, CSS, and vanilla JavaScript with the Web Audio API. No build step, no framework, no server, no accounts, no telemetry, no CDN dependencies. One index.html plus app.js plus style.css, opened directly from the filesystem.

Core engine:
- Build an audio graph: two or three generative layers mixed into a master gain, then destination.
- Layer 1: filtered noise bed. White noise buffer through a lowpass biquad, cutoff slowly drifting via a slow LFO.
- Layer 2: pad. Three or four detuned oscillators playing notes from a fixed pentatonic scale, with slow random note changes every 8 to 20 seconds and long attack and release envelopes.
- Layer 3: optional gentle percussive tick, off by default.
- Apply amplitude modulation to the whole mix: a dedicated gain node whose gain is driven by an LFO oscillator. Expose modulation rate in Hz and modulation depth as a 0 to 1 fraction, so gain oscillates between (1 - depth) and 1.
- Add a stereo widener: split into two channels and offset the modulation LFO phase slightly between them.

Presets, as buttons: Focus (modulation 14 to 18 Hz, higher depth), Relax (8 to 10 Hz, medium depth), Sleep (2 to 4 Hz, low depth, darker filter). Presets set the sliders; sliders stay user-editable.

UI: one play/stop button, a master volume slider, per-layer volume sliders, modulation rate and depth sliders with live numeric readouts, and a session timer with 25, 50, and 90 minute options plus a custom field. Timer fades the master gain to zero over 10 seconds when it expires. Show elapsed and remaining time.

Extra: a file input that accepts local audio files and routes them through the same modulation and stereo stage instead of the generators, so the user can modulate their own music. Nothing is uploaded anywhere.

Persist all slider values and the last preset in localStorage. Dark UI, large type, no animations that pull attention. Include a short README explaining the graph, the modulation math, and a blunt note that this is an audio effect and makes no clinical claims.
